extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly; educators and policymakers interested in night schools and comparative education
extracted.subtask_description: Comparative evaluation of night-school systems (New York vs Paris), focusing on program structure, admissions, attendance, pedagogical suitability for adults vs children, and measures of success such as absenteeism and student engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age appropriateness / adult-only policy (Paris)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking Paris as a representative of European methods, we find that no such absurdity is committed there as the establishment of night-schools for children. The name of these institutions implies their mission. They are called 'ecoles d'adultes' and are intended solely for pupils over sixteen years of age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parisian policy: restrict night instruction to pupils over sixteen; avoid children's night-schools because night attendance after daytime labor is unsuitable for minors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hours of attendance limited to two
rubrics_metrics.description: The hours of attendance in the night-schools are limited to two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs typically run two-hour evening sessions to limit fatigue; this is presented as a structural feature distinguishing night schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary choice of subjects in evening high school
rubrics_metrics.description: In the evening high school, although sixteen different books are on the list of studies, choice of subjects is voluntary with pupils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flexibility in subject choice is intended to accommodate adult learners, but the article links voluntary selection to unexpectedly high drop-out/absenteeism among younger students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attendance requirement: present only when classes are in session
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are required to be present only when their classes are in session.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flexible attendance rules permit students to attend only their enrolled classes; this policy interacts with absenteeism and retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission proficiency requirement for evening high school
rubrics_metrics.description: The evening high school is for adults, as a certain degree of proficiency in various studies must be attained for applicants to gain admission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admission standards (academic proficiency) are used to restrict enrollment to those prepared for high-school-level evening instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral fitness examination for applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Two weeks were devoted by teachers to an examination of the moral fitness of applicants for admission — more strictness, the reports tell us, being observed than formerly as to the character of admitted pupils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-academic screening (moral/character review) was used as an admissions filter; as reported, as many were rejected as permitted to attend when stricter standards were applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absenteeism / attendance rate as primary success metric
rubrics_metrics.description: With such apparent liberty in the high school ... the attendance during the second month of the course for 1879 diminished from fifteen to twenty per cent. ... In the primary and intermediate schools the absenteeism among them amounted to sixty-one per cent, of all whose names were placed upon the school registry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attendance percentages and month-to-month retention are used as key indicators of program effectiveness; high absenteeism prompts consideration of policy responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of night-schools for children (fatigue concern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hundreds of young children attend these schools after the labors of the day have ended, being required to do so either by parents or employers; and, as they enter the class-rooms fatigued by such labors, unless the teachers can attract, interest, and instruct them, they will either become drowsy or resort to mischievous acts to keep awake. This simple record is in itself a pathetic protest against a system of children's night-schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument against children's night-schools: physiological and moral costs (fatigue, inattentiveness, mischief) make night instruction for working children inappropriate despite advocates of book-learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher requirement: attract, interest, and instruct fatigued students
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the teachers can attract, interest, and instruct them, they will either become drowsy or resort to mischievous acts to keep awake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructional method must be adapted to fatigued evening pupils; teacher skill in engagement is essential to prevent absenteeism and misbehavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling structure: two classes per evening per teacher (7–8 and 8–9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two classes are instructed each evening by each teacher — the first from seven to eight o'clock, the second from eight to nine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical nightly schedule divides instruction into two consecutive one-hour classes per teacher; this structural detail affects pacing, student choice, and attendance patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of opening and closing formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening and closing formalities, which are distinguishing features of the day-schools, are omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Night schools streamline administrative formalities compared with day-schools, reflecting different expectations and time constraints for evening students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use (and limits) of compulsory measures (truant law) for evening hours
rubrics_metrics.description: Vigorous measures have been suggested to check this deplorable decrease in the attendance of children. Principal among these has been a proposal to enact a truant law, to be enforced during the evening hours. If such a formula were passed, it would be as unavailing as King Canute's edict to the waves. Natural law would prevent its being obeyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement-oriented interventions (truant laws) were proposed to curb absenteeism but are criticized as ineffective given the underlying causes (fatigue, child labor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collection and use of observational facts / experimental inquiry (historical scientific standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: William Gilbert ... in his treatise 'De Magnete' ... brought together a copious store of facts, the result of his own patient investigations, and connected them by a consistent theory, thus starting the science of electricity on a career still full of promise for the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuing careful observation, accumulation of empirical facts, and connecting them into coherent theory is presented as a standard for advancing scientific knowledge (contrast with mere speculation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bacon's 'Natural History' and method of exclusions (methodological standard and critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon's method required the compilation of what he called a 'Natural History'; that is, an exhaustive catalogue of all natural phenomena ... The peculiar efficacy of the 'Exclusiva' was that all 'natures' save one being excluded by a series of skillful experiments from causal connection with the phenomenon under investigation, the residual element is ... proved to be the 'true cause'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains Bacon's proposed method as a prescriptive standard for induction but critiques it as impracticable and logically flawed (a petitio principii), noting that exhaustive cataloguing of nature is an impossible preliminary and that the method presupposes universal knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of foreign correspondence / distributed observation (Royal Society practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Their foreign correspondents acted the part of the 'merchants of light' appointed to enrich the Island of Bensalem with the knowledge of other lands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guideline for building 'Natural History'—use networks of correspondents to gather observations from diverse locales; though some queries collected were later seen as comical, the practice underpinned empirical accumulation.
